warmup.q: A program writes 14 ledger entries to Kafka inside a transaction, a group of writes meant to count together or not at all. Then it aborts, which cancels the transaction. Another program reads that topic with Kafka's default settings. What does it see?
options: Nothing: Kafka deletes the cancelled entries from the log
All 14 entries: by default, a reader doesn't hide cancelled ones
Nothing: the entries only reach the log once the transaction commits
The 14 entries, but only after the transaction's timeout runs out
warmup.why: The entries go into the log as soon as they're sent, before anyone has decided anything. An abort only adds a marker after them. Hiding cancelled entries is the reader's job, and only a reader set to read_committed does it. The default, read_uncommitted, returns everything. The first and third options are the common belief that an abort removes the entries, or that they're never written at all. The fourth section builds this up.

sections.h: A program that copies payments, and the crash that copies four twice
sections.html:
Let's start with the program. The café payments app keeps every card payment in Kafka, a program that stores messages in logs and lets other programs read them. A log here is a list that only grows at the end, like a notebook you never rub out. Each message in it is a record. A log of records with a name is a topic, and ours is called payments. A topic is split into partitions, separate logs that each keep their own order. A record's place in its partition is its offset: 0, 1, 2 and so on.

A second program, the ledger program, reads payments and writes one ledger entry for each payment to another topic, ledger-entries. A program that writes records is a producer, and one that reads them is a consumer. Read a record, work something out, write a record: this shape is so common that it has a name, consume-transform-produce.

The ledger program also needs a bookmark, so that after a restart it knows where to carry on. Kafka keeps it for the program's consumer group, the copies of one program that share the reading. The bookmark is the offset of the next record to read. Saving it is called committing the offset, and Kafka stores it in an internal topic of its own, __consumer_offsets. Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees built this loop.

Count the writes for one batch of payments, the handful of records that one read returns. The entries go to ledger-entries. The bookmark goes to __consumer_offsets. Those are two separate writes, to different partitions and maybe on different machines, and nothing ties them together. The Try-it below shows what that costs. Instance 1, one running copy of the program, writes entries for four of six payments and dies before it commits. Instance 2 takes over from the old bookmark, offset 0, and writes all six again. ledger-entries ends with 10 entries for 6 payments.

You may be thinking, "Producers II turned on the idempotent producer, and that drops repeats." It drops one kind: a batch that the same producer sends twice. The broker, a server that runs Kafka, recognizes the resend by the producer's id and a sequence number. Instance 2 is a new producer with a new id, so to the broker its entries are new records.

Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees fixed this at the far end, with an idempotency key. That's a unique tag for each payment, which the database checks before it applies a change. It still works. Here, though, every reader of ledger-entries would need its own check. The program that keeps balances would need one, and so would the one that writes monthly statements and the nightly job that checks the books add up. Each would keep its own table of tags it has seen.

Both ends of our program are Kafka, so there's a better option. If the entries and the bookmark were one write, all of it or none of it, a crash couldn't leave half a batch behind. A Kafka transaction is that one write. It covers records sent to any number of partitions, plus the group's bookmark, and it commits them (makes them count) or aborts them (cancels them) all together. Next, we'll see the calls that open and close one.

" inside a transaction" : "") + ", then crashed before committing"); // instance 2: same group (and, for txn, the same transactional.id), starts from the committed offset try (var c2 = consumer(input); var p2 = producer(txn ? txnId : null)) { if (txn) { p2.initTransactions(); // aborts what instance 1 left open, and fences instance 1 System.out.println("instance 2: initTransactions() aborted instance 1's open transaction"); p2.beginTransaction(); } System.out.println("instance 2: starts at offset " + c2.position(input)); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = pollAll(c2, 6); long last = -1; for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { p2.send(new ProducerRecord<>(output.topic(), 0, r.key(), "entry:" + r.value())); } else { p2.flush(); c2.commitSync(next); } System.out.println("instance 2: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-5, committed offset " + (last + 1)); } for (String isolation : List.of("read_uncommitted", "read_committed")) { List<String> values = readAll(output, isolation); Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>(); for (String v : values) counts.merge(v.replace("entry:", ""), 1, Integer::sum); System.out.printf("%-16s reader sees %2d entries: %s%n", isolation, values.size(), counts); } } /** Polls until n records have arrived: a first poll on a fresh broker can come back empty. */ static List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> pollAll(KafkaConsumer<String, String> c, int n) { List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = new ArrayList<>(); while (records.size() < n) c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).forEach(records::add); return records; } static KafkaProducer<String, String> producer(String txnId) { Map<String, Object> config = new HashMap<>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class)); if (txnId != null) config.put("transactional.id", txnId); return new KafkaProducer<>(config); } static KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer(TopicPartition input) { var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "group.id", group, "enable.auto.commit", false, "auto.offset.reset", "earliest", "isolation.level", "read_committed", "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class)); c.assign(List.of(input)); return c; } static List<String> readAll(TopicPartition tp, String isolation) { long end; // the log end; a read_committed reader gets there once no transaction is open try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { end = c.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp); } try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "isolation.level", isolation, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); c.seekToBeginning(List.of(tp)); List<String> values = new ArrayList<>(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 10_000_000_000L; while (c.position(tp) < end && System.nanoTime() < deadline) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach(r -> values.add(r.value())); return values; } } }

aside.title: Why not save the bookmark first?
aside.html: Then a crash between the two writes loses work instead of repeating it. Instance 2 would start after all six payments, and the two entries instance 1 never wrote would be missing for good. That's called at-most-once: each payment is handled once or not at all. For money, a missing entry is worse than a repeated one, because a repeat can be found and removed later, and a gap leaves nothing to find. So programs save the bookmark second and live with repeats, which is called at-least-once.

sections.h: One transaction holds the entries and the bookmark
sections.html:
Go back to the address book for a moment. Suppose you copied each address in pencil and moved the sticky note in pencil too. At the end of a batch you'd either ink the whole lot with one stamp, or cross the whole lot out. A visitor who trusts only ink would never see half a batch. That's the idea of a transaction, and Kafka needs three things to do it.

First, a referee who remembers which partitions a transaction has written to, and how it ended. In Kafka that's the transaction coordinator, a job that one of the brokers takes on. It keeps its notes in another internal topic, __transaction_state.

Second, a name. The producer finds its coordinator through the transactional.id you give it, a stable name for one copy of the program, such as ledger-0. It must stay the same across restarts, because that's how Kafka recognizes the next copy of the same producer. Setting it also turns on the idempotent producer.

Third, five calls, in this order:

  1. initTransactions(), once at start-up. The producer registers its id with the coordinator. It gets a producer id and an epoch, a counter that goes up each time a new copy registers (Producers II met both numbers). The coordinator also finishes anything an older copy with this id left open.
  2. beginTransaction(). From here on, every record the producer sends belongs to the transaction.
  3. send(...). The records go to their partitions straight away, like any other record, marked as part of an open transaction.
  4. sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata()). The bookmark joins the transaction. By default a consumer saves its bookmark on its own every few seconds, so the program turns that off with enable.auto.commit=false.
  5. commitTransaction(). The coordinator writes its decision to __transaction_state. Then it writes a COMMIT marker, a small control record, into every partition the transaction touched, including the group's partition of __consumer_offsets. abortTransaction() writes ABORT markers instead.

Step 3 is the surprise, and it's where the pencil picture breaks. The records are in the log, where every reader can reach them, before anyone has decided anything. An abort doesn't delete them. It adds a marker that tells careful readers to skip what came before. Two sections from now, we'll see what readers make of that.

Here is one batch in Java, then the same batch in Kotlin:

Java
producer.beginTransaction();
try {
    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records)
        producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("ledger-entries", r.key(), "entry:" + r.value()));
    producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata());
    producer.commitTransaction();                 // entries and bookmark, together
} catch (ProducerFencedException fenced) {
    throw fenced;                                 // section 5: a newer instance owns the id
} catch (KafkaException e) {
    producer.abortTransaction();                  // nothing of this batch becomes visible
    rewind(consumer, records);                    // seek back: the batch must be read again
}
Kotlin
producer.beginTransaction()
try {
    for (r in records)
        producer.send(ProducerRecord("ledger-entries", r.key(), "entry:${r.value()}"))
    producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata())
    producer.commitTransaction()                  // entries and bookmark, together
} catch (fenced: ProducerFencedException) {
    throw fenced                                  // section 5: a newer instance owns the id
} catch (e: KafkaException) {
    producer.abortTransaction()                   // nothing of this batch becomes visible
    rewind(consumer, records)                     // seek back: the batch must be read again
}

Look at the two catch blocks. A ProducerFencedException means a newer copy of the program has taken over the id, so this one must stop; the last section explains why. Any other KafkaException means this batch failed, so the program aborts and rewinds.

Don't forget the rewind. After an abort, the consumer's position, the place its next read starts, is still past the batch. Reading the batch moved it, as Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees showed. Without a seek back to the batch's first record, the next read returns the following records, and the aborted batch is never written at all. Kafka 4.0 also asks programs to abort when a call inside a transaction times out with a TimeoutException.

Keep transactions short: one batch of reads each. Every transaction costs a few extra round trips to the coordinator, each a message there and its answer back. So one transaction per record would be slow. A long one holds back readers, as we'll see. But first, a worry. The coordinator is one broker, and brokers fail. Next, we'll see what happens to a decision when one does.

sections.h: Who decides: two-phase commit, kept in a copied log
sections.html:
A transaction that touches several partitions on several brokers has a problem we've met before. Some partitions might hear "commit" and others not, if the coordinator dies halfway through telling them.

Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA, in the Transactions track, solved it with two-phase commit. A coordinator first asks each participant, each place that holds part of the data, to promise that it can commit. Then it writes one line in its own log, and that line, the commit point, decides the outcome. In phase two, it tells every participant the result, and keeps trying until each one has heard. Lay a Kafka transaction over it:

Two-phase commit Kafka transaction
The coordinator the transaction coordinator, one broker
The participants every partition the transaction wrote to, plus the group's partition of __consumer_offsets
Phase one: every participant votes no vote: the producer already knows whether each record arrived
The commit point, one line in a log the coordinator writes "prepare commit" to __transaction_state
Phase two: tell each participant a COMMIT marker written into each partition
A participant left waiting, blocking everyone behind it an open transaction, holding back careful readers (next section)

Kafka's designers describe it the same way. Once "prepare commit" is in the coordinator's log, the transaction will commit whatever fails next, and writing the markers is phase two.

Two differences decide how it behaves. First, there's no vote. Every participant is a Kafka partition that already holds the records. If a send failed, the producer knows, and it aborts instead of asking to commit.

Second, the decision can't die with the coordinator. Its log, __transaction_state, is an ordinary Kafka topic with copies on several brokers; The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR showed how those copies are kept. When the coordinator's broker fails, the broker that takes over the copy reads the log back and finishes every transaction it finds half done, markers and all. The two-phase commit lesson found the weak spot of XA, a standard that lets products from different makers share one commit. It was in exactly this place: a coordinator whose log sat on one machine's disk. Kafka keeps the decision in the same copied log it uses for everything else. A commit built inside one system, where every participant speaks the same rules, avoids most of XA's trouble.

What does it cost? Confluent, a company that sells Kafka services, measured it when transactions arrived in Kafka 0.11, in 2017. They sent 1 KB records and ended a transaction every 100 ms. They measured the producer's throughput, the records it sends per second. It fell about 3% against a producer that waits for every copy and keeps records in order (acks=all with one request at a time). Against a producer that waits for one copy and keeps five requests going (acks=1), which can lose records, it fell about 20%.

Two lessons follow from those numbers, and both still hold. The cost is per transaction, so a bigger batch spreads it over more records. And a transaction's length adds to the wait of every careful reader, because nothing in it is visible before the commit. The figures come from a vendor, on a version long gone, so measure your own before you quote them. Next, we'll meet those careful readers.

sections.h: What readers see: markers, gaps and the last stable offset
sections.html:
Let's watch one partition from a reader's side. The TxnDemo Try-it below writes to it with two producers, one that uses transactions and one that doesn't, and prints what two kinds of reader get.

First a transaction writes a and b and commits. The partition now holds a at offset 0, b at offset 1 and the COMMIT marker at offset 2. A marker takes an offset like a record, but a read never returns it, so a reader sees offsets 0 and 1 and then a gap. Next a transaction writes c and aborts: c sits at offset 3 and an ABORT marker at offset 4. Does a reader get c? That depends on one consumer setting.

The setting is isolation.level. The default, read_uncommitted, returns every record, including those of aborted transactions and of transactions still open. read_committed returns only the records of committed transactions, plus every record written without a transaction. In the demo, the default reader got c. So every program that reads a topic written with transactions must set read_committed, or the transaction protects nothing.

A read_committed reader has a second rule. It can't read past the last stable offset (LSO): the first offset of the oldest transaction that is still open. Everything below the LSO is decided; at the LSO, the broker doesn't know yet. In step 4 of the demo, an open transaction writes e at offset 6, and then the plain producer writes f at offset 7. No transaction wrote f, yet the read_committed reader stops at 6 and doesn't see it. Kafka hands out records strictly in offset order, so it can't give out f while e is undecided.

In the address book, that's the visitor who trusts only ink and reads strictly from the top. At the first pencil line, they stop and wait, even if inked lines follow. For this reader, endOffsets, the call that asks where a partition ends, returns the LSO. Its lag, how far it is behind the end, is measured to the LSO too.

That wait is the price of transactions. An open transaction holds back every read_committed reader of every partition it wrote to, for every record behind it. A producer that crashes in the middle of a transaction holds them for up to transaction.timeout.ms (60 seconds by default). Then the coordinator aborts it, unless a new copy with the same id calls initTransactions() first. Bugs used to leave some transactions open forever, with the LSO stuck. They also blocked compaction, the cleanup that keeps only the newest record for each key (Partitions and segments on disk). KIP-890, a Kafka Improvement Proposal (the numbered document in which Kafka's developers agree on a change), added checks on the broker against that in Kafka 4.0.

The stepper replays the ledger program's crash on both partitions: the crash, the abort, the commit, and the LSO moving through them. Next, we'll ask what happens when the crashed copy wasn't dead after all.

stepper.intro: One partition read, one partition written, and two copies of the ledger program with the same transactional.id.

sections.h: A frozen copy wakes up: fencing, and where exactly-once ends
sections.html:
Instance A of the ledger program stops for 40 seconds. Maybe the Java runtime paused it to clean up memory, a garbage-collection pause from Process pauses: when your own program stops the world. Maybe the network cut it off. The consumer group decides A is gone (Consumer groups and rebalancing), and instance B starts with the same transactional id. Then A wakes up and carries on where it was, holding a transaction full of entries that B has already written. A copy of a program that has been replaced but doesn't know it yet is called a zombie.

Kafka stops zombies with the epoch. Each initTransactions() raises the epoch for its transactional id. The coordinator and the partitions' leaders, the brokers that take the writes for each partition, remember the newest epoch and refuse anything sent with an older one. That's fencing. The epoch works as a fencing token, the idea from Leases, locks and fencing tokens. It's a number that only grows, checked by whoever stores the writes, so a holder that was paused can't write after it was replaced.

In the Try-it, A's next send fails with InvalidProducerEpochException, its commit fails the same way, and its abort fails with ProducerFencedException. The only thing left for A is to close. A reader sees A's committed work and B's, and nothing A tried after the fence.

There's a second fence on the reading side. sendOffsetsToTransaction takes consumer.groupMetadata(), which carries the member's generation, a counter the group moves on each time it shares out the partitions again. If A was thrown out of the group, its generation is old, and the coordinator refuses its bookmark even if the transactional ids differ (KIP-447 added this). That's why one producer per copy of the program is enough, instead of one for each partition it reads. Since Kafka 4.0 (KIP-890), the producer also raises its epoch at the end of every transaction. That closes a gap where a late message from an old transaction could land in a new one. It's also why the epoch in the Try-it jumps from 1 to 4 between A's commit and B's.

Now the edge. A Kafka transaction covers records written to Kafka and bookmarks saved in Kafka, nothing else. Suppose the ledger program also asks the card's bank to move the money, or adds a row to a database such as PostgreSQL, inside the loop. On an abort and retry, the Kafka writes vanish from read_committed readers, but the bank call and the row don't. They happen a second time on the retry. Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka. Give everything else an idempotency key. Send the key with the call to the bank, or check it in the same database transaction as the change.

Couldn't Kafka join the database's transaction instead? KIP-939 proposes exactly that, two-phase commit with an outside system, and Kafka's developers have accepted it. As of Kafka 4.4 (October 2026), it hasn't shipped. Its client calls were taken out of the 4.1 and 4.2 releases before they went out, and Kafka 4.4's KafkaProducer doesn't have them. Design as if it doesn't exist.

The usual way to change a database and Kafka together is the outbox pattern. The program writes the business row and a second row, a note that says "send this to Kafka", in one database transaction. A separate program reads the notes and forwards them. The two-phase commit lesson ended on this pattern, and the Stream processing track builds it.

It commits one transaction, opens another, * and then freezes, the way a long GC pause or a network partition freezes a process. Instance B starts with the * same transactional.id. Then A wakes up and carries on as if nothing happened. */ public class ZombieDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("zombie-demo-" + System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000, 0); var a = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(config); a.initTransactions(); a.beginTransaction(); a.send(new ProducerRecord<>(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-1", "A: entry pay-1")); a.commitTransaction(); System.out.println("A committed pay-1 (partition 0 has seen " + epoch(admin, tp) + ")"); a.beginTransaction(); a.send(new ProducerRecord<>(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-2", "A: entry pay-2")).get(); System.out.println("A wrote pay-2 in a new transaction, and freezes"); var b = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(config); b.initTransactions(); // aborts A's open transaction and bumps the epoch: A is now a zombie b.beginTransaction(); b.send(new ProducerRecord<>(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-2", "B: entry pay-2")); b.commitTransaction(); System.out.println("B started with the same id, redid pay-2, committed (partition 0 has seen " + epoch(admin, tp) + ")"); System.out.println("A wakes up:"); try { a.send(new ProducerRecord<>(tp.topic(), 0, "acct-3", "A: entry pay-3")).get(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" send: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } try { a.commitTransaction(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" commit: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } try { a.abortTransaction(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" abort: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } a.close(Duration.ZERO); // fenced: the only thing left to do b.close(); admin.close(); try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "isolation.level", "read_committed", "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); c.seekToBeginning(List.of(tp)); List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 5_000_000_000L; while (seen.size() < 2 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach(r -> seen.add(r.value())); System.out.println("a read_committed reader sees: " + seen); } } static String epoch(Admin admin, TopicPartition tp) throws Exception { List<ProducerState> producers = admin.describeProducers(List.of(tp)).partitionResult(tp).get().activeProducers(); return producers.stream().map(p -> "producer id " + p.producerId() + " epoch " + p.producerEpoch()).collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); } }

refs.title: Commit removing the KIP-939 two-phase-commit APIs from the 4.2 branch

opening:
Picture copying the addresses from an old address book into a new one, keeping your place with a sticky note. You've copied four when the doorbell rings. While you're away, a friend carries on from the sticky note, which still marks the start. Now four addresses are in the new book twice.

The café payments program does the same. It reads card payments from Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read. It writes a line for each in the ledger, the book of money movements, then moves its bookmark. A crash in between, and payments land in the books twice.

It's easy to trust a setting called exactly-once to fix this everywhere. Kafka has one, and the name sounds like a promise.

In Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters, we accepted that a crash repeats work. In this lesson, we'll make the ledger lines and the bookmark one write, stop a frozen copy of the program, and find where the promise ends. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a sticky note that stayed behind while four addresses were copied twice. A Kafka transaction writes the lines and moves the note as one. Careful readers see the whole batch or none of it, and a frozen copy of the program can't write after it was replaced. The promise stops at Kafka's edge.

With the lab's broker running, list the transactional ids it knows: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-transactions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 list. Each one is a copy of a program that writes in transactions. Ask of every program that reads its topics: does it set isolation.level=read_committed?

Next, we'll let many readers share one partition, each taking single records like jobs from a counter, and see what changes when Kafka runs for real.

compare.note: The same calls in the same order. The order of the catch blocks matters in both languages: ProducerFencedException is a kind of KafkaException, so it must be caught first, or the code would try to abort with a producer that has been fenced. Kotlin builds the bookmark map with associateWith, where Java fills a HashMap in a loop. Neither commits through the consumer. The bookmark travels inside the transaction, which is why the consumer has enable.auto.commit=false and never calls commitSync.

worked.title: Make the fee program exactly-once inside Kafka, and safe outside it

steps.say: Sort the errors the way the KafkaProducer documentation does. Some are fatal, and the producer can't go on: ProducerFencedException, OutOfOrderSequenceException, UnsupportedVersionException and AuthorizationException. Close the producer and let the program restart. Any other KafkaException, including a TimeoutException, can be aborted: abort, rewind, and try the batch again. In the lab, LedgerTransformer.processOnce does this, and a test against a real broker checks the fenced path.

Now the edge. If the fee program also posts each fee to a billing service over the internet, that call isn't in the transaction, and an abort and retry posts it twice. Send the payment's idempotency key with the call, so the billing service recognizes the repeat. The Kafka transaction looks after the fees topic and the bookmark; the key looks after the rest.

lab.title: Model a partition's last stable offset, then build the transactional ledger loop
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 16 fail at first. TxnPartitionTest needs no broker. LedgerTransformerTest uses MockConsumer and MockProducer, stand-ins for the real clients that run in memory and understand transactions. TransactionsOnBrokerTest runs against a real Kafka 4.4 broker in Docker.

In TxnPartition.kt, write a model of one partition. append adds a record, and a record written in a transaction opens its producer's transaction if none is open. The private end, behind commit and abort, gives the marker the next offset and remembers the offsets an aborted transaction covered. Then write lastStableOffset, and read for both isolation levels. Several tests replay the TxnDemo run offset for offset.

In LedgerTransformer.java, write init and processOnce: begin, send the entries, sendOffsetsToTransaction with consumer.groupMetadata(), commit. On a ProducerFencedException, rethrow it untouched. On anything else, abort, seek every partition of the batch back to its first record, and rethrow.

Run everything until all 16 pass. The broker tests check that an aborted batch is hidden from read_committed and visible to read_uncommitted, that the retried batch appears exactly once, and that a second copy with the same transactional id fences the first.
hints: In the model, keep a map from producer id to the first offset of its open transaction. The LSO is the smallest value in it, or the log's end when the map is empty.
read_committed hides a record if its producer's aborted range contains its offset. Neither reader ever gets a marker.
Catch ProducerFencedException before RuntimeException: it extends KafkaException, which is a RuntimeException.

drill.title: The transactional batch from memory
drill.prompt: Write one batch of consume-transform-produce inside a transaction, from memory: begin, send one entry per record, add the bookmark with the consumer's group metadata, commit. If the producer was fenced, rethrow. On any other KafkaException, abort and rewind. Then answer: an open transaction's first record is at offset 120 of a partition whose log ends at 180. Where does a read_committed reader stop, and what does endOffsets return for it?

answer.html: ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)); if (!records.isEmpty()) { producer.beginTransaction(); try { for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("ledger-entries", r.key(), "entry:" + r.value())); Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> next = new HashMap<>(); for (TopicPartition tp : records.partitions()) { List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> rs = records.records(tp); next.put(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(rs.get(rs.size() - 1).offset() + 1)); } producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(next, consumer.groupMetadata()); producer.commitTransaction(); } catch (ProducerFencedException fenced) { throw fenced; } catch (KafkaException e) { producer.abortTransaction(); for (TopicPartition tp : records.partitions()) consumer.seek(tp, records.records(tp).get(0).offset()); } } // The LSO is 120, the first offset of the oldest open transaction. recap: A program that reads, transforms and writes (consume-transform-produce) makes two separate writes: its output records, then its bookmark. A crash between them repeats output, and the idempotent producer can't help, because the next copy is a new producer.

A Kafka transaction (transactional.id, begin, send, sendOffsetsToTransaction, commit) makes the output and the bookmark count together or not at all. It's two-phase commit inside Kafka: "prepare commit" in __transaction_state decides, and the markers finish it.
Records go into the log before the decision. COMMIT and ABORT markers decide, take an offset each and leave gaps. An abort deletes nothing.
Only read_committed readers hide aborted records, and they stop at the last stable offset, the first offset of the oldest open transaction. The default is read_uncommitted.

initTransactions() raises the epoch, a fencing token, so a zombie copy is refused. After an abort, rewind the consumer. Confluent's 2017 test put the cost at about 3% of a producer's throughput with a transaction every 100 ms.

The limit: exactly-once covers Kafka topics and bookmarks only. A call to another service or a database write inside the loop still needs an idempotency key or an outbox. KIP-939, which would let Kafka join a database's commit, isn't in Kafka 4.4.

explain.prompt: Someone suggests turning on Kafka transactions in the ledger program so that "every payment is posted exactly once". The program reads payments, writes ledger-entries and adds a row to a database for each payment. Explain what transactions would and wouldn't promise, and what else is needed.
explain.answer: Transactions would make the Kafka side all-or-nothing. The entries written to ledger-entries and the group's bookmark on payments would become visible together or not at all, so a crash in the middle of a batch wouldn't leave repeated entries for readers that use read_committed. We'd need a stable transactional.id for each copy of the program, so a restarted copy fences the old one and aborts its open transaction. We'd need a rewind after every abort, and read_committed on every program that reads ledger-entries, or those programs would still see aborted entries. Transactions wouldn't cover the database row. If a batch is aborted and retried, the rows from the first attempt are already saved, and the retry adds them again. So the database side still needs an idempotency key, checked by a unique constraint (a rule that refuses a second row with the same key) in the same database transaction as the insert. Kafka can't join the database's transaction, because the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, hasn't shipped. And open transactions hold back read_committed readers at the last stable offset, so batches must stay short.

deeper.html:
Why the epoch now moves on every commit. Before Kafka 4.0, a transactional producer kept one epoch for its whole life. The request that commits or aborts (EndTxn) carried no sequence number, so a delayed commit or abort could arrive after the producer had started its next transaction and be applied to the wrong one. Jepsen, a company that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, found this in Kafka's own protocol in 2024, while testing Bufstream, a Kafka-compatible product: readers saw aborted records, and some writes were lost (KAFKA-17754). KIP-890's second phase, finished in 4.0 and switched on by the transaction.version feature, raises the epoch at the end of every transaction and lets the broker add partitions to a transaction by itself, which closes that gap. The 4.0 upgrade notes also ask programs to abort on TimeoutException and TransactionAbortableException.

How readers skip aborted records cheaply. A read_committed fetch response carries a list of aborted transactions for the range it returns: producer id and first offset. The consumer drops records from those producers between that first offset and the matching ABORT marker. Brokers keep an index of aborted transactions next to each segment file (the .txnindex file), so they can answer without reading the whole log.

Kafka Streams. Kafka Streams is a Java library for programs that read topics, transform records and write topics. With processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, it runs this lesson's loop for you: one transactional producer per thread, with the input offsets and the program's saved state in the same transaction. Confluent's 2017 test measured its cost too. With a commit every 100 ms, throughput fell 15% for 1 KB records and 30% for 100-byte records; with a commit every 30 seconds, 1 KB records showed no cost. The same edge applies: a Streams program that calls an outside service gets no exactly-once for that call.

Atomic commit inside one system. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, makes the two-phase commit section's point in general. Stream processors such as Google Cloud Dataflow, VoltDB and Kafka keep outputs, state changes and input offsets in one atomic commit by running the protocol entirely inside their own system. That avoids the mix of products that makes XA fragile. They also batch many records into each commit to keep its cost down.
